extracted.intended_audience: scholars and advanced students in philosophy of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in foundations/axiomatization
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria Hilbert (and Mancosu's analysis) uses to evaluate proofs, axiomatizations, model constructions, and the methodological ‘purity’ of methods in foundational geometry and metamathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical existence via consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of a mathematical theory (or of objects introduced into it) is established by furnishing a model and showing no contradiction — e.g. 'Euclidean geometry exists, so long as we take over from arithmetic the proposition that the laws of the ordinary real numbers lead to no contradiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce ideal objects if they produce a consistent extension (model) of the axioms; the question whether such objects 'actually exist' is 'idle' once consistency/model is shown. Use embedding into well-understood theories (like the reals) to justify existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal elements justified by system-relative methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimacy of introducing 'ideal' elements is determined relative to the starting system — 'The terminology of ideal elements thus properly speaking only has its justification from the point of view of the system we start out from. In the new system we do not at all distinguish between actual and ideal elements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ideal/real distinctions as relative to an original domain; in the extended theory there is no intrinsic distinction. Introduce ideal elements when they simplify development or enable fuller theory (e.g. analytic completion of geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use embedding/models for independence and relative-consistency proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove independence of Q from P1,...,Pn (in scheme T1) by finding a map τ to another scheme T2 such that (a) τ(Pi) are theorems of T2, (b) T2 can derive ¬τ(Q), and (c) T2 is not inconsistent; τ preserves logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the general form of the independence/relative consistency argument (Poincaré/Frege lineage). Implement by defining structure-preserving translations τ and demonstrating appropriate theorems/anti-theorems in the target model/theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer base theories with fine descriptive control
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing base theories for metamathematical investigations, favor those over which one has a fine degree of control (for instance, countable theories whose elements can be individually described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base theories with countable or otherwise controllable domains make it easier to build models, analyse derivations, and demonstrate (relative) consistency or independence results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic geometry as metamathematical tool (not an enemy of axiomatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the full panoply of analytic techniques (real/complex analysis and analytic geometry) as instruments for the logical analysis of synthetic geometry; they provide point-by-point and line-by-line control of geometrical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic constructions and algebraic calculations are essential for building precise models and for checking that non-intuitive constructions satisfy axioms; analytic methods serve to prove meta-theorems about theories rather than to reintroduce intuition as primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require finding more primitive conceptual levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert does not automatically seek a more primitive conceptual level as the central goal of foundational investigation; Frege-style reductions are dispensable and often appear as assignments for modelling rather than ultimate definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept multiple, possibly incompatible, axiomatisations or 'assignments' as legitimate foundations; use definitions as tools that make unprovable propositions provable rather than as uncovering a single ultimate primitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of local axioms to establish reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that a conceptual reduction has worked, one needs 'local' axioms (e.g., for the naturals or reals) so that derived objects can be shown to have the correct properties; in practice this means supplying an axiom system rather than mere informal definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting reductions (e.g. geometry → analysis, integers as equivalence classes), provide detailed axioms for the target structure so that theorems about the defined objects can be formally derived and checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of method: appropriateness of means to theorem domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the methods used in a proof are appropriate to the kind of theorem proved (e.g., should a purely planar theorem be proved using spatial axioms?). This is the core 'purity' question — subject methods to critical analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs not only for correctness but for methodological 'fit': whether appealing to higher-dimensional or non-native axioms is warranted, and whether the use of such 'impure' elements can be eliminated or explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate unprovability via explicit non-standard model construction
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a theorem is unprovable from a given axiom group, construct a model satisfying those axioms but falsifying the theorem (e.g., Hilbert's analytic plane with the interval [0,+∞] removed producing non-Desarguesian geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design 'gerrymandered' lines/objects (piecewise definitions, distortions like ellipse/arc compositions) and use algebraic calculation to verify axioms hold while the target theorem fails; precise calculation is essential even when the model is visually intuitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-axiomatization: use theorems as alternative axioms when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem that carries sufficient structural content (e.g., Planar Desargues's Theorem) can be adopted as an axiom in place of other (spatial) axioms; this may render a plane 'embeddable' as a plane in space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a theorem is necessary and/or sufficient for a desired structural property (e.g., orderly incidence of lines and planes). If sufficient, the theorem can replace more 'impure' axioms to achieve the same metamathematical ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay between intuition and analytic precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Although intuition and geometric visualization guide the questions (e.g., seeing Desargues's theorem), rigorous analytic construction/calculation is required to settle metamathematical questions and to show models satisfy axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intuition to motivate constructions but rely on analytic/algebraic verification to ensure models/arguments are correct; the analytic work often 'educates' or re-frames intuition about what is essential in a theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a segment-calculus/coordinatization to generate algebraic structure from geometric axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Define addition and multiplication for segments (and related order relations), show these satisfy field axioms (possibly non-commutative ordered field), then use segment pairs/triples to coordinatize plane and space — thereby transforming geometric axioms into algebraic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure can show how certain geometric theorems (e.g., Desargues) imply algebraic properties and permit the embedding of a plane as a plane in a constructed space; relies on having axioms (or substitute theorems) that permit segment operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative treatment of Archimedean axiom and targeted complementary axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain the Archimedean Axiom as independent when seeking an axiom to achieve point-completeness; avoid hiding or losing its role by choosing completeness axioms that imply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select axioms carefully so that their interactions and the necessity of each for particular proofs can be analysed; many metamathematical investigations concern whether use of the Archimedean Axiom is necessary in specific theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design congruence axioms to avoid physico-spatial superposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace arguments that rely on physical manipulation (lifting, turning, superposition) with formal congruence axioms (e.g., the Triangle Congruence Axiom) so triangle congruence criteria (like SAS) are legitimized without spatial intuitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formal axioms are available to justify congruence criteria, proofs avoid appeals to physical movement; evaluate whether the congruence axioms suffice or whether implicit geometric/spatial assumptions remain.
